title_en: Alan Turing: The Man Who Thought About Thinking
title_ru: Алан Тьюринг: человек, который думал о мышлении
description_ru: Биография математика, взломавшего «Энигму» и заложившего основы информатики и вопроса о машинном разуме, и трагедия его последних лет.
text:
In the summer of 1936, a young mathematician at Cambridge published a paper so abstract that few of his colleagues grasped what he had done. Its title, "On Computable Numbers", sounded like a footnote to a footnote. Yet the machine it described, an imaginary device that read and wrote symbols on an endless strip of tape, was the theoretical ancestor of every computer now in existence. Its author, Alan Turing, was twenty-four.

He was born in London in 1912, while his parents, a colonial civil servant and his wife, were home on leave from India, and he spent much of his childhood in the care of foster families on the south coast of England. Teachers found him baffling. At Sherborne School he was praised for his mathematics and criticised for his handwriting, which resembled the trail of an inebriated spider, and for a general indifference to anything that did not interest him. One report grumbled that he was wasting his time. What his teachers failed to see was that he was teaching himself relativity from a textbook that he had borrowed.

At Sherborne he formed the first great attachment of his life, with a fellow pupil called Christopher Morcom, who shared his enthusiasm for science. Morcom died suddenly of tuberculosis in 1930, and the loss marked Turing for good. Later he would wonder, in earnest if unorthodox terms, whether a mind could exist apart from the body that housed it, a speculation that shadowed his later thinking about machines.

At King's College, Cambridge, he was elected a fellow at only twenty-two. The question he tackled came from the German mathematician David Hilbert: could there exist a mechanical procedure that decides, for any mathematical statement, whether it is provable? Turing's answer was no, and the elegance of his proof lay in imagining a simple device that follows instructions, then showing what such a device can never do. A few months earlier the American logician Alonzo Church had reached the same conclusion by a different route, and Turing travelled to Princeton to work with him, earning a doctorate in 1938.

When war approached, he was recruited by the Government Code and Cypher School at Bletchley Park, a Victorian mansion north of London that became the hub of British codebreaking. The Germans enciphered their messages with the Enigma machine, whose settings changed every day, giving some hundred and fifty million million million possible configurations. Polish mathematicians had already cracked earlier versions, and they generously shared their methods in 1939. Turing built upon this foundation. Leading Hut 8, which tackled the German navy's messages, he designed an electromechanical machine called the bombe that could eliminate impossible settings at high speed, exploiting predictable phrases such as weather reports and the closing salute "Heil Hitler".

The consequences were immense. Decrypted naval signals allowed convoys to steer around U-boat patrols during the Battle of the Atlantic, and historians continue to debate how many lives and how many months of war were saved, though the figures cited run from two years to many thousands of ships. Secrecy, however, meant that Turing could not boast of any of it. He received an OBE in 1946 in a citation that revealed nothing, and his closest neighbours knew him only as an eccentric who chained his tea mug to a radiator and, according to legend, cycled to work wearing a gas mask to relieve his hay fever.

After the war he turned to building the machines he had once only imagined. At the National Physical Laboratory he drew up a design for a stored-program computer, but bureaucratic delays frustrated him, and in 1948 he moved to the University of Manchester. There, in 1950, he wrote what may be the most quoted paper in the philosophy of technology, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence". It opens with a disarming question, "Can machines think?", which Turing promptly replaced with a practical test: could an interrogator, communicating through typed messages, reliably tell a machine from a human being? He called it the imitation game. We know it as the Turing test.

His curiosity was never confined to one field. In 1952 he published a mathematical account of how patterns such as the spots of a leopard or the stripes of a zebra might arise from chemical reactions, a founding work of what is now called morphogenesis. He was also a formidable athlete, running a marathon in about two hours and forty-six minutes, a time that would impress many serious club runners today.

That same year, his life unravelled. Homosexual acts were then a crime in Britain, and after he reported a burglary the police learned of his relationship with a young man. Turing was prosecuted for gross indecency and, to avoid prison, agreed to a course of hormone injections intended to suppress his desire. His security clearance was withdrawn, closing the door on the work that had defined him. In June 1954 he was found dead at home, having eaten an apple laced with cyanide; an inquest ruled it suicide, although some friends have always maintained that the death was accidental.

Recognition arrived painfully late. In 2009 the prime minister, Gordon Brown, issued a public apology for the way Turing had been treated, and Queen Elizabeth II granted him a royal pardon in 2013. A 2017 law extended the same relief to thousands of other men convicted under the old statutes, and in 2021 his portrait appeared on the Bank of England's fifty-pound note. Perhaps the most fitting tribute, however, is the one we deliver daily: every time a machine answers a question we have typed, it is carrying on a conversation that Turing began.

questions.question: What did Turing's 1936 paper describe?
questions.answer: An imaginary machine that read and wrote symbols on tape.

questions.question: What was the bombe designed to do?
questions.answer: To eliminate impossible Enigma settings quickly.

questions.question: What is the imitation game?
questions.answer: A test of whether an interrogator can tell a machine from a human.

questions.question: How was Turing treated unjustly in 1952?
questions.answer: He was prosecuted for homosexuality and given hormone injections.
